content:
Yesterday we saw Yahweh offer to destroy Israel and make Moses into a great nation, and we saw Moses plead for the people. We ended with a difficult question. Yahweh said He visits the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, yet He also says the son shall not bear the guilt of the father. How can both be true? Today we find the answer.

Scripture is very clear that Yahweh does not punish innocent children for the sins their parents committed. In Ezekiel 18:20 Yahweh says, "The person who sins is the one who will die. The child will not be punished for the parent's sins, nor the parent for the child's sins." And in Deuteronomy 24:16 He commands, "Parents must not be put to death for the sins of their children, nor children for the sins of their parents. Those deserving to die must be put to death for their own crimes." Every person stands before Yahweh responsible for his or her own response to Him. So, the phrase about visiting the sins of the fathers does not mean that Yahweh holds a child guilty for a wrong the child never did.

What, then, does the word "visit" mean? It means that Yahweh allows the consequences of a parent's sinful choices to continue into future generations, when those generations continue in the same rebellion. Sin rarely affects only one person. An idol-worshipping father often raises idol-worshipping children. A violent father often influences his children toward violence. An immoral home often leaves deep wounds that reach even the grandchildren.

The consequences of sin spread through the family. God is not arbitrarily punishing innocent descendants. He is judging a family line that continues in the same hatred toward Him. And notice the last words of the verse: "of those who hate me." The judgment falls on a family that keeps walking in the same rebellion, not on a child who turns to Yahweh in faith.

Consider a simple example. Imagine a father becomes a drunkard. His children may grow up in poverty, fear, and broken relationships, and those effects may continue into the grandchildren. The children suffer because of the father's sin. But if one son repents, trusts Yahweh, and walks in righteousness, the cycle is broken. This is exactly what Scripture teaches. And we must never forget the very next words Yahweh speaks, for in the same passage He says He shows "unfailing love to a thousand generations of those who love me and obey my commands" (Exodus 20:6). Judgment reaches to the third and fourth generation, but mercy reaches to a thousand generations. The emphasis is always on His abundant mercy, far more than on His judgment. His love reaches far further than His anger ever does.

Now there is a second question hidden in this passage that we must also answer. Moses spoke to Yahweh and pleaded with Him and even seemed to change what Yahweh had said He would do. So we may ask: can a man give advice to God? Does Yahweh need our counsel? Scripture answers plainly that no one can advise God. Paul writes, "For who can know the Lord's thoughts? Who knows enough to give him advice?" (Romans 11:34). And Isaiah says, "Who is able to advise the Spirit of the Lord? Who knows enough to give him advice or teach him?" (Isaiah 40:13). These verses teach us that Yahweh never lacks wisdom. He never learns something new. He never overlooks a fact.
He never needs human advice.

So what was Moses doing? Moses was not informing Yahweh of something He did not know. Moses was not saying, "God, I have a better plan." Instead, Moses was appealing to Yahweh's own character and to His own promises.

Notice what Moses said. He said, "Yahweh is slow to anger and filled with unfailing love... forgive the sins of this people" (Numbers 14:18-19). Moses was really saying, "Lord, act according to Your own revealed nature." Think of it this way. A lawyer in a courtroom does not tell the judge how to be a judge. Instead, he appeals to the law that the judge himself upholds. In the same way, Moses appealed to Yahweh's covenant, Yahweh's glory, Yahweh's mercy, and Yahweh's promises. He was not correcting Yahweh. He was standing on Yahweh's own word.

Then why did Yahweh allow this conversation at all? Because Yahweh had already chosen Moses to be Israel's mediator. Again and again throughout the books of Moses, Yahweh invites Moses into His purposes. At another time Yahweh even said, "Now leave me alone so my fierce anger can blaze against them" (Exodus 32:10). It almost sounds as though God is asking Moses not to pray. Yet Moses prays. Why? Because God was drawing Moses into the work of intercession. God was not discovering whether Moses cared. He already knew Moses' heart. He was revealing that heart, and preparing Moses to act as the mediator who stands between Yahweh and the people.

And this is the most beautiful truth of all. In standing between a guilty people and the judgment they deserved, in pleading on the ground of Yahweh's own mercy, in refusing personal honour so that the people might be spared, Moses was a shadow of someone far greater. Moses was pointing forward to Christ, the true and perfect Mediator, who stands between Yahweh and His people and ever lives to intercede for them. How Moses pictures Christ, and what that means for us as the New Creation, we will study tomorrow.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,
We thank You that You are just, and that You judge no child for a sin he did not commit.

We thank You that Your mercy reaches a thousand generations, far beyond Your anger.

Break in us every sinful cycle passed down to us, and let us walk before You in righteousness.

Teach us to pray as Moses prayed, standing not on our worth but on Your own revealed character.

We do not come to advise You, but to plead Your promises and rest in Your unfailing love.

"The LORD is righteous in everything he does; he is filled with kindness." Psalm 145:17

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
